content: The standard is designed to protect workers during a 10-hour workday and a 40-hour workweek over their working lifetime. 3. 4. The standard is measurable using validated, reproducible, and accessible techniques for both industry and government agencies. 5. Current technology is sufficient to enable compliance with the recommended standard. 6. The standard will be periodically reviewed and revised as necessary. 7. Phosgene is defined as either gaseous or liquefied phosgene. 8. Synonyms for phosgene include carbonyl chloride, carbon oxychloride, chloroformyl chloride, and CG (a military designation). 9. 10. 11. Procedures for sampling, equipment calibration, and environmental sample analysis must follow methods specified in Appendices I and II or equivalent methods in terms of precision, accuracy, and sensitivity. 12. Comprehensive preplacement and annual medical examinations must be provided to all workers exposed to phosgene unless professional medical judgment indicates otherwise based on emergencies, work period variations, or preexisting health conditions. 13. Medical examinations should include comprehensive or interim medical and work histories, with particular attention to pulmonary function. 14. Preplacement and follow-up pulmonary function tests must include forced vital capacity (FVC), one-second forced expiratory volume (FEV1), and forced mid-expiratory flow (FEF). A preplacement chest X-ray is also required. 15. 16. 17. 18. Proper medical management must be provided for workers overexposed to phosgene. 19. 20. Overexposed individuals should avoid unnecessary physical exertion and be transported to medical facilities for assistance. 21. Pressurized oxygen and trained attendants must be available for individuals in respiratory distress. 22. In cases of skin or eye contact with liquid phosgene, contaminated clothing must be removed immediately, and the affected areas flushed with copious amounts of water. 23. 24. Respiratory protection must be readily available for emergencies. 25. Inhalation incidents require immediate removal of the victim to an uncontaminated atmosphere, administration of artificial respiration if breathing stops, and avoidance of physical exertion. 26. Liquid contact incidents require immediate flushing of skin or eyes with water and removal of contaminated clothing. 27. Warning signs indicating the presence of phosgene and its extreme health hazards must be posted in visible locations near areas where phosgene is stored, handled, or used. 28. Emergency entry into hazardous areas requires respiratory, eye, and skin protection. 29. Respiratory protection equipment must be located in specific, easily accessible locations. 30. Unauthorized personnel must be prohibited from entering hazardous areas. 31. 32. First aid procedures must be included in training and posted in the workplace. 33. 34. Workers must be advised that detecting the odor of phosgene indicates the need for immediate corrective action or evacuation. 35. Supervisors must be thoroughly informed of phosgene hazards and participate in worker education. 36. Emergency procedures must be prearranged and include plans for evacuation, transportation, medical assistance, and technical advice. 37. Phosgene leaks must not be treated with water due to accelerated corrosion risks. 38. Phosgene emissions should be directed to an alkali scrubber or neutralization system. 39. Leaking phosgene containers should be positioned to control gas discharge until the leak is managed. 40. 41. Ventilation systems must prevent phosgene accumulation, maintain concentrations within recommended limits, and remove phosgene from workers' breathing zones. 42. Ventilation systems must discharge to the outside air through sorption or decomposition systems and undergo regular maintenance and cleaning. 43. Phosgene must be stored in unoccupied, ventilated, cool, and dry areas, shielded from sunlight and moisture. 44. Storage rooms must have inspection windows for viewing without entry, and other materials should not be stored with phosgene. 45. Phosgene containers must be frequently inspected for leaks and deterioration. 46. Written operating instructions and emergency medical procedures must be posted where phosgene is handled or used. 47. 48. Safety valves and vents for phosgene equipment must discharge through absorbers or neutralizers. 49. Personnel must not work alone when phosgene is first admitted to a system or during leak repairs. 50. Approved eye, skin, and respiratory protection must be worn when handling phosgene containers and systems. 51. 52. Any odor of phosgene must be reported immediately, and the area evacuated. 53. Work areas where phosgene is stored, piped, handled, or used must have eyewash fountains and safety showers readily accessible and in good working order. 54. Enclosed phosgene work areas must have at least two remote exits for emergency escape. 55. Unauthorized personnel must be prohibited from entering areas where phosgene is handled or used. 56. Phosgene installations should be outdoors whenever possible; if indoors, workers should operate from a pressurized control room supplied with fresh air. 57. Appreciable discharges of phosgene must pass through a decomposition system, such as a scrubbing tower with sodium hydroxide or ammonium hydroxide. 58. Entry into confined spaces containing phosgene must be controlled by a permit system, with permits signed by an authorized representative certifying adequate preparation and precautions. 59.
